entities.name: American Communist Party
entities.label: Institution
entities.summary:
The Communist Party USA (CPUSA), founded in 1919 by members of the Socialist Party of America who supported the Bolshevik Revolution, was at its height in the 1930s-1940s one of the most influential radical organizations in American political history — organizing industrial unions, leading anti-fascist movements, providing the backbone of the CIO labor federation, and running Progressive Party candidate Henry Wallace for president (1948) — before being decimated by McCarthyism, the Cold War, and the 1956 Soviet crimes revelations.

The CPUSA's most significant contributions to American life came not through electoral success but through labor organizing (party members were key organizers in the 1930s steel, auto, and electrical workers' unions), civil rights advocacy (the CPUSA defended the Scottsboro Boys in 1931, championed Black equality before it was mainstream, and had significant African American membership), and cultural production (party members and fellow travelers included Paul Robeson, Lillian Hellman, Richard Wright, and numerous Hollywood figures).

McCarthy-era repression (the Smith Act prosecutions of party leaders, the Hollywood blacklist, FBI surveillance) effectively destroyed CPUSA's mass influence by the mid-1950s. Nikita Khrushchev's 1956 'Secret Speech' revealing Stalin's crimes caused further mass resignations. Today CPUSA exists as a tiny organization with perhaps 5,000 members. But its historical role — in building industrial unionism, advancing Black civil rights decades before the mainstream, and providing an organized left during the New Deal era — gave American labor and civil rights movements a significant leftist infrastructure that shaped 20th-century US politics.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: The Communist Party USA — building American industrial unionism, advocating Black civil rights decades early, producing major cultural figures, and being the central target of McCarthyism — shaped 20th-century American labor, civil rights, and political repression history far beyond its modest electoral success.
